title: Calculate useful pixel measurements
intro: Learn NumPy vectorization, broadcasting, Boolean masks, source-preserving transformations, axis aggregation, missingness, percentiles, seeded simulation, dtype overflow and ROI summaries. Credited Witz/HPA published PNG is used as real display-pixel context, never raw calibrated fluorescence.

scientific_context.caution: Thresholds and ROI means computed on synthetic values or rendered RGB do not identify verified nuclei, exophers or fluorescent intensity.

chapter_method: Predict → Run → Investigate → Apply → Prove using genuine NumPy arrays and source-preserving code.

goals.title: Use vectorized NumPy operations
goals.why: Pixel-wise transformations should operate on arrays rather than hardcoded scalar loops.
explain: NumPy ufuncs such as `np.sqrt` and array arithmetic apply to all elements and preserve shape.
A mathematical transform can change a signal scale. It should not silently rewrite the original pixel array.
Never interpret a transformed display pixel as calibrated fluorescence merely because a formula is mathematically correct.

worked_example.code:
import numpy as np
x=np.asarray([1,4,9],dtype=float)
print(np.sqrt(x).tolist())

goals.title: Apply broadcasting with known axes
goals.why: Subtracting a per-channel background from the wrong axis can corrupt measurements even without raising an error.
explain: Broadcasting expands compatible dimensions; for a rows×channels table, a 1D channel background aligns with the final dimension.
A `(rows,1)` divisor or offset applies per row instead. Shape annotations and explicit `[:,None]` reduce mistakes.
Validate the biological meaning of axes before applying the mathematically allowed broadcasting rule.

goals.title: Make Boolean masks that respect missingness
goals.why: A missing score must not be silently treated as a failed biological sample or a real zero measurement.
explain: A Boolean mask is an array of True/False positions. Conditions can be combined with `&` and parentheses.
Convert optional numeric values to float and use `np.isfinite` before threshold comparison; None becomes NaN in an appropriate float array.
A threshold identifies numerical candidates only; it is not a validated object classifier.

Mask values are computed quality rules on numerical data; a selected region is not automatically a validated cell.

goals.title: Aggregate image values over an explicit axis
goals.why: A channel mean, per-row mean and field mean answer different questions.
explain: NumPy reductions such as `np.mean` collapse a chosen axis, producing a shape based on the remaining axes.
For `(rows,cols)` data, `axis=0` aggregates down rows to per-column means. `axis=1` aggregates across columns to per-row means.
Decide the scientific unit before aggregating; microscope fields are not automatically independent replicates.

goals.title: Handle NaN and missing numerical records
goals.why: An absent signal measurement must be excluded transparently rather than converted into zero.
explain: None may become NaN in a float NumPy array. `np.isfinite` separates observed numeric values from missing, infinite or invalid entries.
Compute an arithmetic mean over finite values, explicitly returning `None` when no observations remain.
The missingness mechanism itself may bias a biological result. A computational mean cannot justify ignoring systematic exclusions.

worked_example.code:

arr=np.asarray([2,None,4],dtype=float)
valid=arr[np.isfinite(arr)]
print(valid.mean())

goals.title: Use percentiles and ranks responsibly
goals.why: Different threshold choices can give very different candidate counts on the same field.
explain: `np.percentile` computes an interpolated empirical percentile. It is not automatically the brightest 25% as an integer count.
Sorting an array reveals ordered values but loses original spatial positions unless indices are kept separately.
A 75th percentile of pixel values is a numerical criterion, not a universally validated biological segmentation threshold.

goals.title: Avoid overflow and precision traps
goals.why: Unsigned image data can wrap around when arithmetic exceeds the storage range.
explain: `uint8` stores 0–255; adding 10 to 250 in uint8 arithmetic wraps instead of producing 260, so promote dtype before arithmetic.
Use an integer type with sufficient range for sums and a float dtype for noninteger means. Inspect `np.iinfo` and `np.finfo` rather than guessing precision.
Saturation in a raw detector and overflow in a processed array are distinct problems requiring different diagnostics.
